name: Deutsche Bank

summary.text: Deutsche Bank AG is a Frankfurt-based global bank. On January 30, 2017, the New York State Department of Financial Services fined it $425 million and required an independent monitor over a 'mirror trading' scheme in which clients bought Russian stocks in rubles in Moscow while related parties sold the same stocks for dollars through the bank's London branch, with trades cleared in New York, moving about $10 billion out of Russia. The UK Financial Conduct Authority fined the bank £163 million the same month for anti-money-laundering control failings between 2012 and 2015, its largest AML penalty. In May 2017 the Federal Reserve imposed a $41 million penalty and cease-and-desist order over the U.S. operations' Bank Secrecy Act/AML program, and in July 2023 a further $186 million for violating its 2015 and 2017 orders.

facts.claim: On January 30, 2017, NYDFS announced a $425 million fine on Deutsche Bank AG and its New York branch, and required the bank to engage an independent monitor, for allowing traders to run a money-laundering scheme using 'mirror trades' among its Moscow, London and New York offices that improperly shifted $10 billion out of Russia. DFS said the bank missed numerous opportunities to detect, investigate and stop the scheme because of extensive compliance failures, and that it occurred while the bank was on notice of serious compliance issues dating back a decade. DFS worked with the UK FCA.
facts.quote: The bank allowed traders to engage in a money-laundering scheme using "mirror trades" that improperly shifted $10 billion out of Russia. [...] DFS's investigation found that the bank missed numerous opportunities to detect, investigate and stop the scheme due to extensive compliance failures.

sources.publisher: New York State Department of Financial Services
sources.title: DFS Fines Deutsche Bank $425 Million for Russian Mirror-Trading Scheme

facts.claim: Deutsche Bank's own SEC filing says that under its settlement with DFS it entered into a consent order, agreed to pay civil monetary penalties of $425 million and to engage an independent monitor for up to two years; the filing puts the FCA penalty at about £163 million and records a May 2017 Federal Reserve settlement with a $41 million penalty.
facts.quote: Under the terms of the settlement agreement with the DFS, Deutsche Bank entered into a consent order, and agreed to pay civil monetary penalties of U.S.$ 425 million and to engage an independent monitor for a term of up to two years.

sources.publisher: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (Deutsche Bank AG Form 6-K, Exhibit 99.1)
sources.title: Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft Form 6-K (FY2018), Exhibit 99.1

facts.claim: In January 2017 the UK FCA fined Deutsche Bank £163 million for failing to maintain an adequate anti-money-laundering control framework between 2012 and 2015, the largest penalty the FCA or its predecessor the FSA had imposed for AML control failings. The FCA said the bank was used by unidentified customers to move about $10 billion of unknown origin from Russia to offshore accounts.
facts.quote: The bank was used by unidentified customers to move about $10 billion of unknown origin from Russia to offshore accounts.

sources.title: FCA fines Deutsche Bank £163 million for serious anti-money laundering controls failings
Final Notice to Deutsche Bank AG (Firm Reference Number 150018)

facts.claim: The FCA found that between April 2012 and October 2014 the front office of the Russia-based subsidiary, DB Moscow, executed more than 2,400 pairs of mirrored trades, which customers used to move more than $6 billion from Russia, through Deutsche Bank in the UK, to overseas accounts including in Cyprus, Estonia and Latvia; a further $3.8 billion in suspicious one-sided trades was also identified.
facts.quote: Between April 2012 and October 2014, the front office of the Russia-based subsidiary, DB Moscow, executed more than 2,400 pairs of mirrored trades. Customers used these trades to move more than $6 billion from Russia, through Deutsche Bank in the UK, to overseas accounts, including in Cyprus, Estonia, and Latvia.

sources.title: FCA fines Deutsche Bank £163 million for serious anti-money laundering controls failings
Final Notice to Deutsche Bank AG (Firm Reference Number 150018)

facts.claim: The FCA found breaches of Principle 3 and SYSC rules 6.1.1 R and 6.3.1 R; Deutsche Bank settled at an early stage and received a 30% discount (the penalty would otherwise have been £229,076,224), and £9.1 million of commission earned from the suspicious trading was disgorged within the penalty. The FCA noted that the Central Bank of Russia and NYDFS also took action in December 2016 and January 2017.
facts.quote: Without the discount, the penalty would have been £229,076,224. [...] The Central Bank of Russia and the New York Department of Financial Services also took action against the firm in December 2016 and January 2017, respectively.

sources.title: FCA fines Deutsche Bank £163 million for serious anti-money laundering controls failings

facts.claim: On May 30, 2017, the Federal Reserve Board announced a $41 million penalty and a consent cease-and-desist order against Deutsche Bank AG, finding that its U.S. banking operations failed to maintain an effective program to comply with the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money-laundering laws; the order (signed May 26, 2017) cites deficiencies in transaction monitoring that prevented proper assessment of BSA/AML risk for billions of dollars of potentially suspicious transactions processed between 2011 and 2015 for certain European affiliates.
facts.quote: Deutsche Bank's U.S. banking operations failed to maintain an effective program to comply with the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering laws. [...] deficiencies in the U.S. operations' transaction monitoring prevented proper assessment of BSA/AML risk for billions of dollars in potentially suspicious transactions processed between 2011 and 2015 for certain affiliates in Europe.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board announces $41 million penalty and consent cease and desist order against Deutsche Bank AG
Order to Cease and Desist and Order of Assessment of a Civil Money Penalty, Deutsche Bank AG

facts.claim: In July 2023 the Federal Reserve imposed a $186 million fine and a new consent order on Deutsche Bank for violations of the Board's 2015 and 2017 consent orders relating to sanctions compliance and anti-money-laundering controls.
facts.quote: Federal Reserve Board announces two enforcement actions against Deutsche Bank AG, its New York branch, and other U.S. affiliates

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board announces two enforcement actions against Deutsche Bank AG, its New York branch, and other U.S. affiliates

facts.claim: CNN reported on November 15, 2017 that a U.S. Justice Department investigation into Deutsche Bank's role in the $10 billion Russian mirror-trading scheme had gone dormant in the months after the bank's January 2017 settlements with regulators, noting that such criminal investigations can span months or years before a resolution is reached or the department decides there is no case.
facts.quote: a Justice Department investigation into Deutsche Bank's role in a $10 billion Russian money laundering scheme has gone dormant months after the bank settled with regulators

sources.title: DOJ probe on Russian trades through Deutsche Bank quiet

facts.claim: Deutsche Bank's annual reports on Form 20-F describe the matter as equity trades entered into by certain clients with the bank in Moscow and London that offset one another; the filings say the bank's internal review found certain violations of its policies and deficiencies in its control environment, and that it took disciplinary measures against certain individuals.
facts.quote: certain violations of Deutsche Bank's policies and deficiencies in Deutsche Bank's control environment

facts.claim: CNBC reported on November 3, 2020, citing unnamed sources, that Deutsche Bank had been the Trump Organization's biggest lender, financing more than $2 billion in loans to Donald Trump during his business career; that the bank first started lending to Trump in the late 1990s; and that he still owed it at least $130 million according to his latest financial disclosures.
facts.quote: Deutsche Bank has been the Trump Organization's biggest lender, financing more than $2 billion in loans to the president during his business career

facts.claim: In April 2019 Donald Trump, three of his children and the Trump Organization sued Deutsche Bank and Capital One to block them from complying with subpoenas from the House Financial Services and Intelligence Committees for records of Trump's finances; the committees' stated aims included an investigation into Russian money laundering. A federal district judge denied a preliminary injunction.

sources.title: Trump sues Deutsche Bank and Capital One to block House subpoenas for his financial information

sources.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (via Justia)
sources.title: Trump v. Deutsche Bank AG, No. 19-1540 (2d Cir. 2019)

facts.claim: On December 3, 2019 the Second Circuit (Trump v. Deutsche Bank AG, No. 19-1540) affirmed in substantial part the denial of a preliminary injunction, holding that although the plaintiffs showed irreparable injury they had not shown a likelihood of success on their statutory and constitutional claims, and ordered prompt compliance subject to procedures on nondisclosure of sensitive personal information; Judge Livingston dissented in part. The Supreme Court stayed the subpoenas on December 13, 2019 and consolidated the case with two others.
facts.quote: they did not show a likelihood of success on any of their statutory and constitutional claims

facts.claim: On July 9, 2020, in Trump v. Mazars USA, LLP (consolidated with the Deutsche Bank case), the Supreme Court held that presidents are not immune from congressional subpoenas and set out a four-part test for evaluating subpoenas seeking information about the president.

facts.claim: CNN reported on December 22, 2020 that Rosemary Vrablic, a Deutsche Bank private banker it described as a trusted contact to the Trump Organization and Jared Kushner, had taken over the bank's lending relationship with Trump on the private-banking side after its commercial lending division stopped doing business with him, and that she and colleague Dominic Scalzi had resigned from the bank effective at the end of 2020. Bloomberg reported in February 2023 that Vrablic, a former managing director who arranged hundreds of millions of dollars in loans to Trump's company, had been subpoenaed by Trump in the New York attorney general's civil fraud suit.
facts.quote: took over the bank's lending relationship with Trump on the private side after the commercial lending division stopped doing business with Trump

facts.claim: On July 7, 2020 NYDFS announced a $150 million penalty on Deutsche Bank AG, its New York branch and Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas under a consent order covering the bank's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein (August 2013 to December 2018) and correspondent relationships with Danske Bank Estonia and FBME Bank. Deutsche Bank's Form 6-K says the order found violations of New York banking law in connection with those three former client relationships, and the bank paid the penalty in the third quarter of 2020.
facts.quote: Deutsche Bank AG, its New York branch, and Deutsche Bank Trust Company America (collectively "Deutsche Bank" or the "Bank") have agreed to pay $150 million in penalties

facts.claim: The DFS consent order found that Epstein was onboarded in 2013 without escalation to the Americas Reputational Risk Committee, contrary to bank policy; that on January 24, 2014 the bank opened accounts for The Butterfly Trust knowing a beneficiary was an alleged co-conspirator in Epstein's prior offenses; that over 120 wires totaling $2.65 million went to trust beneficiaries; and that conditions set by the committee in January 2015 were not transmitted to most of the relationship team and were misinterpreted by a compliance officer.
facts.quote: Conditions imposed by a Bank reputational risk committee were not transmitted to the majority of the account relationship team and were misinterpreted by a compliance officer.

CEO Christian Sewing told staff in an internal memo that taking Epstein on as a client in 2013 was a 'critical mistake'.

facts.claim: On October 20, 2023 Judge Jed Rakoff gave final approval to Deutsche Bank's $75 million settlement of a class action by Epstein's accusers, covering women abused or trafficked from August 19, 2013 until Epstein's death; the bank did not acknowledge wrongdoing, and Rakoff approved attorney fees of 30%.
facts.quote: Rakoff, who granted preliminary approval for the deal in June, signed off on the settlement during a court hearing in Manhattan.

openQuestions: Period: the FCA dates the mirror trades to April 2012 - October 2014 (AML framework failings 2012-2015); the Federal Reserve order refers to transactions 2011-2015. The site's '2011-2016' window is wider than either.
The DFS consent order text itself was not retrieved; the DFS press release and Deutsche Bank's 6-K are cited.

The $186 million figure and the reference to the 2015 and 2017 consent orders in the July 2023 Federal Reserve action come from the search tool's summary of the Fed's 19 July 2023 release, not from a verbatim passage; confirm against the release.

DOJ mirror trades: no charging decision, declination or closure announcement was found. The fiscal 2020 Form 20-F still described a DOJ investigation as ongoing with an undisclosed provision; the search tool's summary of the fiscal 2021 20-F indicated that filing no longer refers to an ongoing DOJ investigation and says only that the bank has advised regulatory and law-enforcement authorities in several jurisdictions including the United States. Confirm against the fiscal 2021 and later 20-Fs before stating the investigation ended. A Bloomberg piece carried by Gulf News ('Deutsche Bank wasn't only mirror trader, Russian central bank says') also described the DOJ probe as open; its date was not shown.

Trump lending: the 'more than $2 billion' figure comes from a November 2020 CNBC report citing unnamed sources, not from a filing or court record; the passage was returned alongside that result and its attribution to that article should be confirmed. The Second Circuit opinion was not opened for its own description of the lending relationship. The site's 'over $300M' figure was not found. Justin Kennedy (named on the site as head of DB real-estate securitization) was not researched; no source for his role was opened.

Rosemary Vrablic: 'rosemary-vrablic' is an id in public/data/entities.json and is used as the connection target; CNN's description of her role was returned in summary form and should be checked against the article.

Epstein items appended 2026-10-09: the consent-order date is July 6, 2020 (order) vs. July 7 (announcement/6-K). The DFS order PDF was not opened in full; the Butterfly Trust and wire figures come from DFS release/order excerpts. A third-party site's claim that $75 million of the $150 million was attributable to Epstein was not found in DFS or Deutsche Bank documents and is not recorded.
